chunks: As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi', he said:

I wrote to the one who was asked about a ghedir (pool) in which rainwater collects and from which water is also drawn from a well — a person performs istinja in it from urine or excrement, or the junub (one in a state of major ritual impurity) performs ghusl in it. What is its minimum hadd (threshold) below which [its use] is not permissible?
He wrote back: 'Do not perform wudu from the like of this except out of necessity.'

This report is interpreted as indicating a type of juristic disapproval (karaha), because were it not so, the water of the ghedir would either be less than a kurr — in which case it becomes najis and its use is not permissible under any circumstance, and the obligation would be tayammum — or the intended amount would be more than a kurr, in which case it does not carry impurity and is not restricted to cases of necessity. The correct interpretation of this narration is karaha, because in the presence of waters whose purity is certain (mutayaqqan), it is not appropriate to use these waters; they are to be used only when [pure] water is entirely unavailable.

key_terms.التَّيَمُّمَ: tayammum — dry ablution performed with earth when water is unavailable or forbidden to use
key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَةُ: karaha — juristic disapproval/dislike (makruh); a ruling below outright prohibition
key_terms.الْكُرِّ: kurr — standard volume of water (approx. 384 litres) sufficient to resist ritual contamination in Shia fiqh

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia jurisprudential ruling on performing wudu from a pool used for istinja and ghusl by the junub?
ai.summary: This hadith, transmitted by al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi', records a written question posed to the Imam about a pool (ghedir) that collects rainwater and well-water and is used for istinja and ghusl, to which the Imam replied that wudu from such water is only permissible in cases of necessity. Sheikh al-Tusi, the author of al-Istibsar, interprets this ruling as indicating juristic disapproval (karaha) rather than absolute prohibition, reasoning on the basis of the kurr standard that the restriction applies only as a preference for waters of certain purity when they are available.
